subject: Copywriting
title: Clickbait: Headlines as Traps
description: One-minute skill: Clickbait: Headlines as Traps.

hook.text: 'You Won't Believe What Happened Next'—a headline formula that generated billions of clicks and ruined trust.

buildup.text: Upworthy and BuzzFeed proved curiosity gaps work. Withhold information and people click to fill the gap.

discovery.text: Clickbait exploits a psychological itch. Your brain can't tolerate incomplete patterns. You MUST click.

twist.text: Facebook and Google changed their algorithms to punish clickbait. The technique that worked too well got banned.

climax.text: Clickbait taught a lesson: short-term tricks destroy long-term trust. Headlines must deliver on their promise.

punchline.text: Clickbait got the click. Then lost the reader forever.

quiz.question: What psychological principle does clickbait exploit?

details.summary: Clickbait headlines promise sensational content that the article fails to deliver. 'You Won't Believe What Happened Next' became the defining format of mid-2010s internet content. While clickbait initially drove massive traffic, it eroded trust and triggered platform algorithmic changes that...
details.whyItMatters: Understanding clickbait reveals where curiosity-driven headlines cross into manipulation. The backlash against clickbait reshaped platform algorithms and reader expectations permanently.
takeaways: Clickbait creates curiosity gaps that the content fails to satisfy
Short-term traffic gains came at the cost of long-term audience trust
Platform algorithms now penalize clickbait, favoring accurate headlines

faq.question: What makes a headline clickbait versus merely compelling?
faq.answer: The difference is delivery. A compelling headline creates curiosity and then satisfies it with quality content. Clickbait creates curiosity and disappoints. The test is simple: would a reader feel rewarded or cheated after clicking? Clickbait fails that test consistently.

faq.question: Why did platforms crack down on clickbait?
faq.answer: User satisfaction metrics declined as clickbait proliferated. Facebook measured that users who clicked clickbait spent less time reading and engaged less with the platform afterward. Penalizing misleading headlines improved overall user experience and kept people on the platform longer.
